summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon. The criminal provision introduced in 2019 was repealed in 2020, and no offence covering same-sex conduct is in force.

Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence. Article 402 placed 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

The provision was applied. Two men were arrested under it within months of its entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men accused of conducting a same-sex wedding in December 2013 and released them, four years before any statute addressed same-sex conduct.

Repeal began on 23 June 2020, when the National Assembly voted 48 in favour, 24 against with 25 abstentions, and continued with Senate approval on 29 June and presidential signature on 7 July 2020. The reversal divided public opinion.

The age of sexual majority is 15 for girls and 18 for boys, regardless of the sex of the partner. Before 2020 the thresholds were unequal, at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts, so both the historic and current thresholds are keyed to sex rather than to the sex of the partner.

The constitution ratified by referendum on 16 November 2024, with more than 90 per cent approval on turnout of about 55 per cent, codifies privacy in Article 18 and rejected civil-society demands to restore the criminal offence. Article 16 defines marriage as a union between two people of opposite sex, effective 12 April 2025, and is entrenched as unamendable. The text was adopted under the military government that took power in August 2023, ending 56 years of rule by the Bongo family.

A trans visitor should expect no legal gender recognition in Gabon. There is no procedure for changing gender markers on identity documents, and the law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity.

Enforcement directed at gender presentation runs through general public order provisions. Police are reported to occasionally bring breaches of modesty charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentation and against same-sex couples, and this misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread. State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present, while harassment by private individuals is described as common. Societal stigmatisation of LGBTQ+ people is documented.

LGBTI organisations cannot register as associations in Gabon, which removes the formal civil-society bodies that would otherwise document abuses and provide support to visitors.

Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023, amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, treats sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data. Gender identity is not covered by that protection.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gabon. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot marry or have the partnership recognised, and the constitutional marriage definition forecloses recognition by ordinary legislation.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 constitution was drafted and ratified under the military government that took power in August 2023, which ended 56 years of rule by the Bongo family. Its privacy guarantee and its marriage definition were settled by the same process: campaigners who sought the restoration of criminalisation were refused, and the exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage was written in as unamendable.

Because the marriage definition cannot be amended, partner recognition for same-sex couples is not reachable through ordinary legislation in Gabon. Any change would require the replacement of the constitutional text.

Gabon's 2019 offence did not derive from a colonial penal code that the country carried over at independence in 1960. The lawfulness that preceded 2019 and that has applied since 2020 is the longer-standing position of Gabonese law, and the criminalisation episode ran for about twelve months.

Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has no reported enforcement record. Whether the privacy guarantee changes police conduct toward LGBTQ+ people is not evidenced by any case in the source inventory.
localsOnly:
Gabonese law offers no route to legal gender recognition, so residents who transition hold identity documents that record the sex assigned at birth.

LGBTI organisations are unable to register as associations. Residents therefore lack the registered civil-society bodies that would otherwise provide services, legal support and public documentation of abuses.

Involuntary conversion practices, described as both religious and ritualistic, are reported as widespread in Gabon. The sources record no legal prohibition of these practices and no enforcement action against them.

Harassment of LGBTQ+ people by private individuals is described as common, while state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is not prohibited by law.

Police are reported to occasionally use breaches of modesty charges against residents with non-gender-conforming presentation and against same-sex couples.

The age of sexual majority is set by sex at 15 for girls and 18 for boys regardless of the sex of the partner, replacing the earlier thresholds of 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts.

Sexual orientation and sexual life are treated as sensitive personal data under Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023, which amended Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011. Gender identity is not among the categories that provision covers, and same-sex couples have no recognition, including marriage.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative practice exists for changing gender markers on Gabonese identity documents is unresolved in the sources; they record only that no legal gender recognition is available.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence data for Gabon, and no comparison with the general violent-crime rate. The level of risk of violence faced by trans visitors relative to other visitors is not sourced.

How the sex-keyed age of sexual majority thresholds are applied to a person whose legal record and appearance differ is not addressed by any source in the inventory.

The description of breaches of modesty charges as occasional and not widespread carries no date in the inventory, so current enforcement frequency is not established.

The 2019 US State Department human rights report for Gabon is inventoried as documenting the criminalisation year and societal discrimination; its specific findings are not reproduced in the inventory and are not restated here.

Entry rules, visa practice and screening at Gabonese ports of entry are not covered by any source in the inventory.

Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has no reported application, and its practical effect on police conduct, custody or documentation procedures is unresolved.
